title: The second pledge
hook: seventy-three men and two women pledge to protect him as their own

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mus'ab the teacher. Your line was: the first teacher. Did you pass on a line to someone, and leave them free with it? Day seven hundred sixty-one.

Another pilgrimage. Another night at Aqaba. But this time it's after dark, a third of the night gone, and people are slipping away from their sleeping companions one or two at a time, Ibn Ishaq says, creeping like birds. They gather in a ravine. Ibn Ishaq counts them: seventy-three men and two women. One of the women is Nusayba bint Ka'b, known as Umm Umara. They've come to make a different kind of promise than the twelve made a year before. Today: the second pledge.
screen: `AFTER DARK, IN A RAVINE.` → `SLIPPING AWAY ONE BY ONE.` → `SEVENTY-THREE MEN, TWO WOMEN.`

segments.voice: The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, comes with his uncle al-Abbas, who, Ibn Ishaq says, still followed the religion of his people but came to look after his nephew. Al-Abbas speaks first, and he's blunt. He is safe among his own clan. If you're going to take him, be sure you can protect him. If not, leave him now. Then the Prophet recites the Qur'an to them, and asks for their pledge: that they protect him as they protect their own women and children. Al-Bara ibn Ma'rur takes his hand and says yes: we are people of war and weapons. Then another man, Abu al-Haytham, raises a hard question. We have ties with other people in Yathrib, and we'll be cutting them. If we do this, and God gives you victory, will you go back to your own people and leave us? And the story says the Prophet smiled, and answered: no. Blood is blood. I am of you and you are of me. I will fight whom you fight, and make peace with whom you make peace. Look at what's changed from the first pledge. That one was about conduct. This one is about bodies and homes: we will stand in front of you. And it runs both ways. They ask for his loyalty as clearly as he asks for theirs. Their reward, he tells them, is paradise. In the story, no wealth is promised, and no power. Only that.
screen: `AL-ABBAS: PROTECT HIM OR LEAVE HIM.` · `AS YOU PROTECT YOUR OWN.` · `WILL YOU LEAVE US LATER?` · `I AM OF YOU, YOU ARE OF ME.` · then, large: `PROTECT HIM AS YOUR OWN.`

segments.voice: The practice: be someone's protector. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people you already protect without thinking: a child, a parent, a partner, a friend. Now widen it by one. Who in your life is exposed right now, and has nobody standing in front of them? A new kid at school. A coworker who gets talked over. A neighbor living alone. Hold that person for a moment. Then picture one ordinary, concrete thing you could do to cover them this week: walking with them, speaking up, checking in. Keep it small enough to actually do. If you pray, you can ask God to keep them safe. The bell holds the time.
The second pledge. At night at Aqaba, men and women of Yathrib promised to protect the Prophet as their own families, and he promised he was theirs. Today's word.
Your line: protect him as your own. Today, do the one small thing that puts you between someone exposed and whatever's coming at them. Day seven hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: Muslims remember the second pledge of Aqaba as the promise that opened the way to Medina, and honor the Ansar, the helpers of Medina, for keeping it.

fork.setup: you're Abu al-Haytham. you're about to cut ties at home for this man. what do you ask him?
options: will you leave us once you win?
fork.reveal: he asked if the Prophet would go back to his own people. he smiled: I am of you and you are of me.

trapdoor: what you thought: a second copy of the first pledge.
what it means: this time they promised to protect him with their lives, and he promised to stay with them.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Ishaq's account of the second Aqaba: al-Abbas's warning, al-Bara ibn Ma'rur, Abu al-Haytham's question, and the answer, I am of you and you are of me.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the second Aqaba: seventy-three men and two women; al-Abbas speaks; the pledge to protect him as their women and children; al-Bara ibn Ma'rur; Abu al-Haytham's question; 'I am of you and you are of me'; paradise as the reward)

notes: Count of seventy-three men and two women, 'a third of the night gone', and 'creeping like birds' are from Ibn Ishaq as recalled; confirm.
Abu al-Haytham's question refers in Ibn Ishaq to ties with 'the men' (often understood as the Jews of Yathrib); written here as 'other people in Yathrib'. Confirm.
All dialogue paraphrased; confirm especially 'blood is blood' and 'we are people of war and weapons'.
Editor pass: replaced the stock line 'the question nobody wants to ask' with 'a hard question'; reworded 'the whole trade' so it doesn't anticipate tomorrow's 'profitable trade' line about Suhayb.
Original game set to null; no single Arabic word fit the day better than yesterday's bay'a (used on day 759).

Audit pass: match pair 'al-Bara ibn Ma'rur: took his hand first' replaced with 'people of war and weapons'. Ibn Ishaq records rival claims to the first handclasp (al-Bara, As'ad ibn Zurara, Abu al-Haytham), so 'first' was a contested superlative.
